units.title: HTML: the document, text, links, images, landmarks, forms, and tables
units.intro: Everything we build this semester is a web page, so we start with the language of pages. This week you will type a document from its skeleton up: headings and paragraphs, lists, links and images with text alternatives, the landmarks that give a page its regions, a form whose fields have labels, and a table. Each step shows the page the browser draws from your markup and the tree it built from it, so you can see that HTML is structure, not appearance; the appearance comes next week.
localNotes: Set up VS Code and a local preview on your own computer this week, as the Week 2 setup guide describes; every page in the lab can also be downloaded and opened from a folder.

units.title: CSS: selectors, the cascade, the box model, and Flexbox
units.intro: In Week 3 we wrote the structure of a page and left it in the browser's default look. This week you will style it. You will select elements by tag, class, and id, watch the cascade decide between two rules that disagree, measure the box model with and without box-sizing, and lay out a row of cards with Flexbox, reading the main axis and the cross axis off the result. Every step edits a stylesheet linked from the page, the way a real project does.

units.title: Grid, responsive layout, and the first JavaScript
units.intro: The page from Week 4 has a layout; this week it gets one that adapts, and then it gets a script. You will build a page layout with Grid, add a breakpoint and check it at a narrow width, and then open the console pane and meet JavaScript: variables and types, strings, operators and the coercion surprises they hide, and your first functions. Every value you print this week becomes something you put on the page in Week 6.

units.title: Arrays, objects, the DOM, and events
units.intro: In Week 5 our scripts printed values to the console. This week they reach the page. In Session 1 you will loop over arrays, transform them with map and filter, and group related values into objects. In Session 2 you will select elements from the page, change their text and classes, create and remove elements from data, and respond to a click, including the one mistake nearly everyone makes with addEventListener. By the end, a button on the page changes what the page shows, and you can explain the order in which your code ran.

units.title: Delegation, data attributes, storage, and asynchronous JavaScript
units.intro: Week 6 ended with a page that responds to clicks on elements that were there from the start. This week the page handles elements it creates later, remembers its data across a reload, and waits for things it does not have yet. In Session 1 you will handle a whole list with one listener, carry an id on each element with a data attribute, and keep the list in localStorage with the safe load pattern. In Session 2 you will trace synchronous and asynchronous code, wait for a promise with then and then with async and await, and make your first fetch for JSON, checking the response before you read it. Finish the DOM and events topic first; the fetch topic continues it.
localNotes: The lab's "Run, keeping saved data" button plays the part of a reload; on your own computer, open the Application panel in DevTools to see the stored JSON and edit it by hand.

units.title: CourseHub: application architecture
units.intro: Everything from Weeks 3 to 7 comes together in one application. This week you will build CourseHub, the book search with bookmarks, as a sequence of small typed edits: components that return markup, a search form, bookmark buttons handled by one listener, storage that survives a reload and refuses bad data, a real request with every outcome shown on the page, and then the reorganization that Session 1 described, one state object that the whole page is rendered from. The last step reads the finished file by responsibility and sets it beside the React version of the same ideas, which is where Week 10 begins.
localNotes: The Week 8 notes build the same application from empty files with Live Server and a Git history on your own computer; the lab starts you from the finished structure and style so the behavior, data, and architecture get the time.

units.title: Fetch, request states, and verification
units.intro: In Week 7 we made a request and read its JSON. This week the request becomes a feature a user can trust. You will show the four states every request has, loading, success, empty, and error, build a search URL from what the user typed with encodeURIComponent, and cause every failure on purpose with the fixture controls: an HTTP error, a body that is not JSON, and a dropped connection, with a sentence for each. You will also refuse a second request while one is pending, which is the first of the stale-result bugs the React weeks grade. Run every fetching step on fixtures, on a real preset, and on a custom base, and read the network pane each time.
localNotes: Choose a public API for your own search project this week and confirm with the Custom base URL entry that it answers requests from the browser; a server that refuses shows a CORS message in the console, which is a server setting rather than a bug in your code.
